name: Brilliant
line: Brilliant teaches in interactive concepts and tests at checks. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous.
description: AMP vs Brilliant: Brilliant teaches in interactive concepts with a check at the end. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Brilliant teaches through short concepts built from interactive problems, and it assesses at checks: a diagnostic at signup, a skill check after each concept, and unit checks [4][6][7]. In AMP, assessment is continuous: every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem. Each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer, and learned skills keep returning in practice.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem. Brilliant places a learner with a short diagnostic at signup, and jumping ahead takes a passed level check [7]. After that it assesses at checks: a skill check at the end of each concept, and unit checks across a unit [6].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem in front of the learner: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Brilliant the unit is the concept: a short run of interactive problems that often poses a question before showing the method, and ends in a skill check [4][6]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [15].

reasons.title: Hints from tested code
reasons.body: AMP runs no AI model while a learner works. Every problem, hint and explanation comes from tested code, and answers are checked exactly. Each hint gives the first step and never the answer. Brilliant's tutor, Koji, is built partly on a third-party language model. It sees the problem, asks guiding questions and is designed not to hand over answers [5].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts as learned when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. An answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In Brilliant a skill check ends each concept, and a unit check uses a map of prerequisite skills to find the gap behind a miss [6]. We found no stated rule in its published pages for when a skill counts as learned [6]. AMP's rule is open source: open to peer review and contribution.

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Brilliant says important ideas return across sessions, and names spacing and interleaving among its methods [4]. Its review runs through unit checks, which reach back to earlier material, and missed problems add review lessons to the learner's plan [6]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [14].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, from counting through precalculus, on one map of skills. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels. Brilliant sets a recommended order of topics [10]. Its math begins with fractions at about grade 4, and it says it does not present a complete arithmetic sequence for kindergarten through grade 3 [2].

rows.range: From fractions at about grade 4 to the opening topics of calculus. No complete arithmetic sequence for kindergarten through grade 3 [2].
rows.start: A short diagnostic at signup picks a starting topic. Jumping ahead takes a passed level check [7].
rows.teaching: Short concepts built from interactive problems, often a question before the method [4]. Koji, an AI tutor, asks guiding questions [5].
rows.next: A recommended order of topics [10]. Practice uses the learner's history to pick problems [4].
rows.mastery: A skill check ends each concept [6]. No stated rule for when a skill counts as learned found in the pages we read [6].
rows.review: Ideas return across sessions [4]. Unit checks reach back to earlier material, and misses there add review lessons [6].
rows.print: Lessons need an internet connection and are not available offline [11].
rows.adult: None required. Built for learners who work independently [9]. Homeschool families keep their own records [3].
rows.reports: A parent dashboard: days active, problems solved, accuracy on checks. It says it is not a grade [8].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [12][13].

theirs: Brilliant teaches math, coding, data science and science through short interactive lessons [1]. Its math runs from fractions at about grade 4 to the opening topics of calculus [2]. It describes itself as a fit for learners who work independently, and says it is not a complete K-12 school [9][3].

A short diagnostic at signup picks a starting topic [7]. A learner then works through short concepts built from interactive problems: move a point, test a pattern, estimate, choose a strategy [4]. Each concept ends with a skill check. Unit checks cover the unit and earlier material, and use a map of prerequisite skills to find the gap behind a miss [6]. Koji, an AI tutor, can see the problem, ask guiding questions and sketch on the screen [5].
credit: Interactive problems that ask a learner to act and reason before the method is shown [4].
Unit checks that trace a miss back to the prerequisite skill behind it [6].

theirs: We found no study of Brilliant's effect on math achievement on its website, in Evidence for ESSA, or among the What Works Clearinghouse's intervention reports [12][13].

Brilliant's own figures come from an analysis of middle and high school learners who asked Koji for help: 94% tried again, 66% then answered correctly without Koji giving the answer, and 87% of those who moved on got the next problem right [9]. Brilliant calls these behavioral signals and says they are not a substitute for a controlled academic study [9]. The analysis describes no comparison group.
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% on the researchers' own test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [14]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve math performance [15]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want interactive, visual puzzles that pose a question before the method.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or still building arithmetic.
You want every problem, hint and explanation to come from tested code.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Brilliant?
questions.answer: Brilliant teaches in short interactive concepts and assesses at checks: a diagnostic at signup, a skill check after each concept, and unit checks [6][7]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Brilliant work?
questions.answer: We found no study of Brilliant's effect on math achievement on its site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [12][13]. Its published figures track behavior inside the app, and Brilliant says they are not a substitute for a controlled study [9].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
